utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in court. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we please have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis and Aditya Menon for the Prosecution, assisted by our case managers, Alma Imamovic and Fraser McIlwraith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to my colleagues from the OTP, to everybody in and around the courtroom. I'm Vasvija Vidovic, with Nicholas Robson, with our legal assistant Lejla Gluhic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Yes, I see the witness is not in court. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has a number of hopefully brief submissions concerning upcoming witnesses, and we would ask to address the Trial Chamber in private session concerning these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Buljubasic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yesterday, before you started your testimony, you made a declaration to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. I just remind you that you are still bound by that declaration. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Buljubasic. Yesterday --

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, we talked about the duties of your Cabinet, and I would like to continue with that topic. You would agree with me, would you not, that in 1995, the international community made substantial efforts to stop the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: General Delic was a negotiator on behalf of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very frequently, these were long-term negotiations within Bosnia and Herzegovina and outside; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: During 1995, after the signing of the Washington Agreement between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were frequent negotiations about many questions with the Croats in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in 1995 negotiations and agreements were still being conducted with the HVO of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I personally attended talks attended also by the commander in Kresevo and Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You would agree with me that those negotiations occupied a large measure of General Delic's time and attention; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And peace depended on the outcome of those negotiations, lasting peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, because those negotiations led to the Dayton and later the Paris Agreement and the cessation of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were also various international conferences in 1995, peace conferences as well as donor conferences; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is correct is that General Delic was more involved in all of these matters rather than combat actions; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that the general dealt with all these matters, but I cannot say -- and I say again I don't have an overview or any record of where he went and how much time he spent in these places in order to give you a proper answer. But everything you have said so far is correct, that General Delic was quite engaged and that this required a lot of time for the talks, the travels.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that it was a task of Mr. Delic's Cabinet also to correspond with units to appoint, and you said this does not include communications about combat actions. Here I refer to paragraph 7.3 of your statement, and I would like to ask you this in relation to that: The communications between the general's cabinet and you, as the Chef de Cabinet, were limited as regards this type of matter, about what the Staff and the administration's relocation to Kakanj in connection with combat activities?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because an operations centre was formed in Kakanj which directly communicated with units and received combat reports from the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to put some questions to you now about documents shown to you by the Prosecutor. Could the witness now look at document PT2477, please. And you commented already on this document. The witness did that in paragraph 38 of the statement. For the transcript, before we see the document, we're talking about a BBC report from the 4th of September, 1995. Witness, can you please look at the Bosnian version of the document. You will probably recall this document. It refers to the fact that General Delic was a member of the delegation that visited the Islamic Republic of Iran, and according to this document the visit took place from the 28th until the 31st of August. You said that you remember that the general was away at that time; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that the general went on this visit. I saw this document in English. I did not see it in Bosnian before. That's the first time that I'm seeing it now in Bosnian. It's true that the general went to visit Iran, and now from the document I see that this was from the 28th to the 31st of August. Of course, I couldn't recall and I do not remember the date. I mean, it was a long time ago. But I do know that he was with the delegation that travelled, and I know that this document, in English, was shown to me before.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, thank you very much. Your Honours, we can put this document away now. Actually, perhaps the document can be given an exhibit number, because ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 818.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just ascertain whether it's PT2447 or P2477, because I think you said one thing on the transcript -- on the microphone and I see another document appearing on your exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2477.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, is that on your list that you have exhibited -- that you have distributed?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a document that was shown to the witness by the Prosecutor, and the witness comments on it in paragraph 38 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could clarify --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Your Honours, excuse me. The mistake is here with us. We made a mistake on the list. The list says "2447". We have the mistake on our list, but it's actually 2477. That's the correct number. I apologise. I didn't notice that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The mystery is solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You may proceed, Madam Vidovic. The document has been given an exhibit number, 818.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About this document, can the witness please be shown D669. For the record, this is an order of the General Staff of the BH Army, and the date is the 28th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement you made a number of references to the commander being represented by General Hajrulahovic. I want you to look at the date, the 28th, the document produced by the General Staff of the Army, dated the 28th of August, 1995, the same date that we saw in that article or paragraph. Were you speaking about Brigadier General Mustafa Hajrulahovic who was representing the general in Sarajevo, standing in for him during his absence?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my statement, I said that there was an organisational order by the army from October 1994, and pursuant to this order the Chief of Staff, the army's Chief of Staff, would also stand in for the commander in terms of his role and function. However, whenever the commander left Sarajevo, there were still commitments remaining in Sarajevo, and one of the administration heads would normally stand in for the commander. Most frequently, this was General Hajrulahovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, can this document be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 819.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you mentioned the fact that General Delic, in September 1995, was away in Malaysia?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 36 of your statement, you state that you believe that Delic had appointed someone to stand in for him during his absence. Based on that, the command-and-control system was fully operational. This was your comment on the video clip that you were shown by the OTP. You recall that, Witness, don't you?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Unfortunately, I don't have sufficient time to show you the clip again, but I do want you to look at Exhibit 621 instead. This is part of a set. The date is September 1995. Right now, I want you to look at page 1 of this document. First of all, this was produced by the Army's General Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the date is the 5th of September, 1995, is it not?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed it is. It was produced in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I just want you to look at this [indicates], the signature representing the commander and Enver Hadzihasanovic. Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I mean, I see where it says: "Representing the commander," but I can't see what else it says, and I don't recognize the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Be that as it may, on the 9th -- on the 5th of September, it is quite obvious that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, interpretation will proceed when the speakers stop overlapping. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're actually asking me General Hadzihasanovic was representing General Delic on that day. Yes, that is quite obvious, if you look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness, thank you. And now could you please go to the last page of this document. The same applies to both the English and the B/C/S. You agree that this document was also produced by the Army's General Staff, that it was produced in Kakanj on the 16th of September, wasn't it? If we could please pull up the Bosnian so that we can see the signature. This document shows, does it not, that on the 16th of September, General Hadzihasanovic was representing the commander?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, but could we just pull the document up a little so that I can see the actual signature?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that's what the copy's like, that's what we were given. All right.

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it reads: "Representing the commander" or standing in for the commander, Brigadier General Enver Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You will agree, won't you, that these documents show that General Rasim Delic was being represented by the Chief of Staff for a time period in September 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did say that in my statement, didn't I? And if you look at the organisational order by the army, you can see that as well. In terms of his function and role and responsibility, the Chief of Staff of the Army must stand in for the commander. Is it always necessary to draw up a special order whenever the commander is away on who exactly stands in for him? Well, this wasn't something that was regulated. Sometimes an order was drafted on who would be standing in, and sometimes it was made explicit in terms of each person's responsibilities. So sometimes when the commander was away, it was quite obvious that he would be represented by the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this explanation, Witness. And now I want to ask you several other questions. Your Honours, this document can now be put away. It has an exhibit number already. And what I wish to ask you now is a number of questions about the situation throughout 1995, about the priorities faced by General Delic throughout that year. Do you agree that in Sarajevo itself, and you were working there, too, throughout 1995, weren't you, the situation was very difficult?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I definitely agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The siege continued throughout 1995 and until it became unbearable for all those residing in Sarajevo; is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. That's when the Markale incident happened as well, the Markale incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You say that's when the Markale incident occurred as well. This was an incident where a single shell killed about 100 people; am I right? ?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, plus over 100 injured.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Civilians were being killed on a massive scale on the streets of Sarajevo, targeted by the Serb artillery, who were besieging the city; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They were trying to wear down the town's defences, and that's why the general launched an operation to try to lift the siege of Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: General Delic was busy planning this operation of which he was in command; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the same time, and we're looking at July 1995, are we not -- right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, late June and early July, the first half of July 1995, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My apologies. At the same time, the pressure on the enclaves of Sarajevo, Zepa and Gorazde was truly horrifying, was it not?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All those living in the non-Serb enclaves were facing massacres, the possibility of being massacred; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Eventually, in July 1995 the Srebrenica tragedy occurred, and it was soon followed by the Zepa tragedy; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this tragedy took up much of the General Staff's attention and focus, including General Delic personally, and all they were thinking about was how to avoid future tragedies of that kind?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite true. There was a lot of domestic pressure across Bosnia because of the tragedy, because of what had occurred in Srebrenica, from the 11th of July onwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that throughout July 1995, those were the priorities that General Delic had to come to grips with?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, especially after Srebrenica, in the second half July, including the best part of August. There was the accommodation problem and everything that the Srebrenica tragedy caused. All those civilians had to be put up somewhere, all those civilians who had left Srebrenica en masse.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you do agree that the fighting continued throughout July and August, leaving thousands of people trying to leave the Srebrenica area; they were being pushed and thousands of them were still being killed, in fact, were they not?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the 11th onwards Srebrenica, and just after Srebrenica, some of Zepa's citizens as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buljubasic, now that we're talking about Srebrenica, about the Srebrenica area, the tragedy also enveloped the following places: Srebrenica, Cerska, Kamena [as interpreted] and Konjevic Polje; is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. I think the Srebrenica tragedy affected Srebrenica alone. As for Cerska, Kamen [as interpreted] and Konjevic Polje, most of those had fallen previously into the hands of the Republika Srpska Army. Srebrenica and the part that had remained back in 1993, after the Srebrenica area had been demilitarised, Cerska, Konjevic Polje and all that area had been taken before, at least as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you're not quite certain, are you? You weren't there, were you?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there. I'm not positive, but as far as I can remember, Srebrenica was reduced to the status of an enclave in 1993, was separated from Zepa. In the meantime, all communication between the two had ceased simply because Cerska, Kamenica and Konjevic Polje had fallen. The continuity of the fighting occurred in Gorazde, and I lost part of the territory around Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record, Your Honours, page 22, line 5, we're talking about Kamenica. Line 4, actually. Page 22, line 4, "Kamenica." Right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Srebrenica, yes, but we're talking about Cerska, and it says "Kamen" instead of "Kamenica," and I really want that word on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, fine, fine. Thank you for all these answers, and now I'll move on to some other questions about paragraph 15 and 16 of your statement, in which you speak about the communications system.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You say that most of the phone lines to Sarajevo had been cut?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. That was at the very outset, because the main -- the principal post office building in Sarajevo had burned down.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You say that a satellite telephone line was being used; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was at Vranica, is the same building where the Cabinet was. There was a satellite line in my statement [as interpreted]. I point out that this was a stationary satellite telephone such is normally used on ships. The size was enormous. It had to be placed somewhere and left there. It was a stationary telephone device. It wasn't a mobile device. Once you put it somewhere, it had to stay right there. It also had a special sort of parabolic antenna which had to be adjusted at a certain angle to meet the satellite in order to establish a line of communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Buljubasic, I have so many questions, please try to keep your answers to a clear-cut yes or no wherever you can. Anyway, thank you very much for this exhaustive explanation. There's something else I want to ask you about this telephone. It's true, isn't it, that communication over this telephone could only be intercepted by electronic devices; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Military Security Service warned the General Staff about the fact that satellite telephone lines were being listened to and intercepted; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, then, won't you, that this sort of communication could not be used for conveying confidential information? It wasn't appropriate for that, was it?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This line was not used for command purposes. This line was used to maintain communications with certain other areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina who were able to use this sort of communication, who had appropriate equipment for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 19 of your statement, you spoke about packet communications; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some people called it "packet communications." Some people called it "paktor [phoen] communications," so those were the expressions I used.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Do you agree that there had to be a certain infrastructure in place for this type of communication to proceed?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The bear minimum required for this type of communication was a coding and decoding device, a keyboard, a monitor, a computer actually, and a KT device that could be used to transmit the signal once the processing had been dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Maintaining this communication was some sort of a user at the command centre and someone who had appropriate equipment for this kind of communication; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There had to be at least one operator present at any time for this type of communication to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that you sent dispatches to the commander via Kakanj whenever he was away from Sarajevo. You don't actually know for sure whether, at the Kakanj command post, they always had appropriate information as to the commander's whereabouts? They didn't always know whether any such information had reached the commander or not, did they?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite right, but that wasn't the case very often. Sometimes whoever deputised for the commander in Sarajevo was perhaps unable to deal with something, and then he would say, "Okay, try to get in touch with the commander". This was not the case very often. As for the fate of those documents that were dispatched to Kakanj, I don't know what became of them because I was not physically able to actually see them through, was I?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Can the witness now please look at D667. This is a document produced by the commander's cabinet. The date is the 14th of February, 1994, and this is about forwarding a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I know that you are not the person who produced this document, rather it was your predecessor, but I do wish to discuss the principle behind this with you. How was mail forwarded from the Cabinet to Kakanj? Look at the introduction, please, and tell me if you agree with this. The document actually says that the Chef de Cabinet, Murat Softic, is forwarding this order to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command so that he can familiarise himself with it, and then once it is signed, it should be passed along. Isn't that what it says? And what I mean to ask you really is, this is exactly the way you continued to work whenever you were the one sending dispatches; right? That is something that you shared with us a while ago, was it?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just below this, below the signature, you see what the substance is of a given document being forwarded. Now please look at the last page of this document. This is a document being submitted to the commander for signature. Can you please look at the last page now. And what I actually mean to ask you is this: This document here is not actually signed by the commander, it's signed by Hadzihasanovic on his behalf; yes?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And now the facts, and that is what I have been meaning to ask you about, and this is something we discussed a while ago, the fact that a document is being forwarded to the commander so that he can familiarise himself with it in Kakanj. This, in itself, doesn't mean that the commander actually ever set eyes on the document, ever received it, ever signed it. At any rate, this would be done on his behalf by whoever was standing in for him at the time whenever he was away; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in terms of the person's function, but this was probably something that just couldn't wait, so whoever was in charge, whoever was on duty, would sign it off.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, may the document please be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 820.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Could this one be put away, please, and I would like the witness to look at E727, Exhibit 727.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday, when you started testifying, we talked about this document -- rather, when I started cross-examining you. And you said that you would obtain from the Military Security Service sealed envelopes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You made a sketch of one such envelope, and you said, "This is a rough sketch, no more than that." In actual fact, you don't really know what sort of documents those envelopes contained, do you? Were these bulletins, was this some sort of special information being passed along, was this just an ordinary letter or something else; you don't really know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I never opened those, I never opened any of those envelopes. It always said "To be opened by the commander, himself." There were all those parcels and envelopes being sent to the commander. It always read "To be opened by the commander alone." Therefore, I never opened those, did I? I never opened them, I didn't know what was inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now do you agree that you would forward such envelopes to the commander whenever he was there, perhaps his secretary, actually? That would be a fair thing to say. That's who you forwarded these envelopes to, because the general actually had two secretaries, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was at the post office. That was where I delivered all the other mail. If the command was there, I would do it then and there. If he was away or he had other commitments and this had to wait, then I would normally leave this with one of the secretaries and they would then forward this to the commander himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That would be Ms. Lemes; right? I think you mentioned her, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and whenever she was away, there was young Haris Kristianovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. What if the general was away from Sarajevo? Do you agree with me that the mail wasn't just waiting for him; the secretary would most probably have forwarded these documents to whoever was deputising for the commander? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know what became of the mail. I don't know whether it was given to whoever was deputising or was being forwarded to wherever the commander happened to be. I just handed it over and I didn't really follow this through. It never really came back to me. Such documents that were sent on their way were never returned to me. Therefore, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you help me with this: If it was returned and when it was returned, how exactly did it get back to you? Through the secretary; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know that the envelopes always read "To be opened by the commander alone." I would give it to the commander and then the commander would see what it was, he would familiarise himself with whatever the contents were of those envelopes. That was for him to do. He would send it back, and he would indicate who the recipient was. As for that type of mail, I know that it was always forwarded back to whoever the recipient was that was indicated on the envelope itself. As for any mail sent through the secretary, I really don't know how it was returned or who it was returned to.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. All right. Be that as it may, you hand over a sealed envelope to one of the secretaries. The general is away, so you have no idea where it goes next or whether it returns?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I don't know how it got to be there in the first place, I don't know who it was returned by. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you about paragraph 20 of your statement. The OTP showed you document 2028. It's actually P2028.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you calling that --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we put this one away, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you calling 2028 or are you just telling him that he saw it?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am calling it up. There are certain things indicated on that document, and I would like the witness to have a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You made certain comments in relation to this document in your statement. I'm sure you remember. I want you to have another look. I would like the witness to be able to see the beginning of page 1. Could we just pull it up slightly, please, so we can actually see the top of the page. Witness, you agree that there is no indication whatsoever that this document was encrypted, is there, above the body of the document, the text, the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. There's some sort of an illegible signature at the top of this document, but I don't see the sort of thing that normally was indicated on whichever documents were encrypted.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's look at the entire page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, you said the Prosecution showed the witness this document. Is it already an exhibit or not? I don't see it on the list of documents shown by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness commented this document in the statement. I don't know what the status is now, but perhaps I would like to hear what the witness has to say about it first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we can see that there are no other indications on this page. Now we can look at the last or the second page of the document. In English, it's the third page, Your Honours. Can we please look at that?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buljubasic, do you agree that the document is not signed and it's not stamped?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's clear from the document that it's not stamped and signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that it could be a draft version that was not actually -- that had not actually seen the light of day?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see any indications that this document was actually sent out by paktor communication, and I cannot tell if it was received, because there is no indication if it was received by anyone, because if it was received, perhaps then it would have some logic that it wasn't signed. But since there is no receipt stamp either, then ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In any case, you personally never saw this document before; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not before the time that I gave my statement, when it was shown to me for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we can put this document away now, and I would like the witness to look at another document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're putting it away because there's no basis for it to be tendered or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not tendering it, Your Honour. This is a document that the witness in the statement -- I am not tendering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please look at document P2188 [Realtime transcript read in error "P2098"] now, please. I will repeat the number. It's 2188, 2188. It's the right document now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You commented this document in a paragraph of your statement. This is a document of the 28th of June, 1995. I would like you to look at page 1 of this document, please. This is an information about the importance of continuing the liberation operation. It's an act by the 3rd Corps. It's quite faint here, but you can see that it is the 3rd Corps Command here. Now, Mr. Buljubasic, would you agree -- can we please scroll down so that we can see the bottom of the page in the B/C/S and in the English version. Actually, in English, it should be on the following page. What I would like to suggest to you and to ask you is that: It is evident that the Deputy Commander for Morale, Husic, is forwarding this document, report on the significance of continuing liberation activities, is passing it further along; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, can you see that there is a line between that, meaning that the act is copied below this line? You've seen that, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beginning of the act is again.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, all right. Can we look at the last page of the document now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Please, can you see that this is Army General Rasim Delic who signed the document, and then it says that the transcript is authenticated by the Assistant Commander for Morale of the 7th Brigade and the name is there. I would, first of all, like to ask you this: Can you please look at these initials here on the left? We can all see that the document is not signed. Can you look at the initials now? Are these the initials of anyone from your Cabinet?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So the transcript is authenticated. Did you ever see, anywhere on the document, that the document was sent to the encryption section? Does it say that anywhere?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the document, there are some shaded parts, so I don't know what's on the accompanying document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we go back to the cover page or the first page so that the witness can look at it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see, above the number, it's either a bad copy or something, but you cannot see the code of the person who dispatched it or the code of the person who received the act. And, secondly, when you compare the first act and the second act, there is something illogical there. If it was the Assistant Commander for Morale of the 3rd Corps, then it's strange that the authentication is carried out by the commander of a brigade. In this other act, which is not signed by General Delic, it's signed by the Assistant Commander of the Brigade for Morale, this is something that is illogical.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the reason why I asked you that. Please, we've seen the general's name, and do you agree that in acts we saw that it's not signed, and even if this document was encrypted, we wouldn't see it until we -- who signed it until we saw the original act?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the encryption section does not convey the signature. Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, between you and the witness, just so that I'm not left behind, what do you mean by an act in this context?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document, Your Honour, which is not an order, so it's a document. It's an order or a report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you talk of an act below and above, a line between, I see one document here, except that at the last page there was a line drawn somewhere and then there were some writings below. I'm not quite sure which is the one act and which is the other act. I'm sorry, I'm asking this question long after the word "act" has been used, so that perhaps may not be very clear. But we can go to the last page and I can show you what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I understand what the dilemma is, because it was the same for me in the beginning. Please, can we scroll down this first page a little bit, and then we'll go to the next page, so that we can see the bottom of this text.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, please, do you agree that here this author, Assistant Commander for Morale, is allegedly sending a copied document of the Army General Staff further on to the units that are mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand. Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see from the act that the Assistant Commander for Morale, Husic, is sending this document or this act to the units that are enumerated here. You can see that on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now we see one line that separates that completely from the second document, which was drafted on the 28th of June, 1995; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And now can we look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It was also drafted on the 28th of June, 1995. It may be at a different time. This one is -- you're talking now about the thing that is done at 9.45? Okay. And that line --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That line divides the two acts?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And based on my understanding of the two documents, the draftee of the first document decided himself to whom he would send the transcripts of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says on the act itself. "Dispatched to" means that it was dispatched to -- each act that has the following words: Dispatched to, and then lists the recipients, means that that document should be delivered to those units that are mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So my question is this: The author of this second document below the line did not decide who the document will be sent to, this document by the Assistant Commander for Morale; we you don't have anything like that stated in this lower document?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but again I'm coming back to this illogical matter. It's not logical, below the line, where it says: "The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, General Staff" and the number, it's not logical that the authentication of an act by the General Staff is done by a person who's on the other side, who's from the brigade. This is what is a discrepancy here. It's not possible for a morale commander in one of the brigades to be verifying the accuracy of an act that originated from the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Just one more question in relation to this act. Please, do you agree that you have never seen this act before, as the Chef de Cabinet of General Delic?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, because there is nothing here indicating an archive number, place of origin, so it was not drafted in the Cabinet and it did not pass through the Cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, can this document be put away now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before that, how do we know that there are two separate acts here and authored by two different people?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please read the first sentence here that we can see on the screen? "Please find attached," is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, please, so that we can look at the first page in the English, so that Their Honours can follow. So can we show the first page of the English version of this document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, Witness.

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Please find enclosed the report of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina General Staff regarding the importance of continuing liberation operations."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there. In other words, enclosed with this act that is signed by this Husic, because this lower act or document is below the line -- is that correct, that is that information, that is something that you can tell by the title?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The usual practice is if lower-ranking units are being sent information from higher-ranking units or commands, then there would be an accompanying or a cover letter that accompanies that act. Since these are two acts that we're talking about, the one on the first page signed by Captain First Class Husic should represent this accompanying act relating to this information that was supposed to be sent out. However, I, as a soldier, have some doubts about the accuracy of this act that goes with this accompanying act and it being signed by an Assistant for Morale from one of the brigades, whereas it says that the act was drafted in the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Your Honours, I think this would be a good time, if you don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll put the question later on, because I'm very sorry, I still entertain some doubts. There are still some very dark areas about these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was probably going to do the same after the break. We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still have a problem with this document, the entire document. If I understood properly, there is a document that was sent by Husic, together with an attachment or annex. Did I understand properly, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This document from Mr. Husic is a cover document, because he's enclosing this other document that is partially below the line and partially on the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of the entire document, we have Husic's letter, together with the attachment, and there is a certification of the authenticity of the entire document; is that right? Can we see the last page, please. Can we scroll down to get to the last page. This is what I wanted to know: Who's signature is it? Is it possible to know? Who signed this certification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of the act, it says that the authenticity is verified by the Assistant of the Commander for Morale, Captain First Class Sulejman Kurtanovic [phoen], if I'm seeing this correctly. This is what I see underneath the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting, but evidently this is a misinterpretation into English, and I can see what the confusion is. It says that the transcript is authenticated by, and the interpreter is interpreting it that the transcript is authentic, and these are two completely different things in our language. Perhaps we can clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, I understood that this authentication meant that the copy was a certified copy of the original. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle, the person that authenticates the transcript asserts that it is true to the original, but this is not something that I am disputing. What is being disputed is the procedure and the way in which these acts are being forwarded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I was trying to understand, this confirmation of the authenticity applies to the entire document, does it, so the letter by Husic together with the attachment or annex? It does not apply only to the document signed by General Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I actually understand it to be the opposite. The authenticity of the transcript refers only to this document, because Husic above writes his own separate act. The procedure is disputable here. If a unit, such as the Corps Command here, received this act --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understood that, because you've said this already twice, and still I have some problems with it. If this was an authentication regarding the entire document, therefore authentication that would apply to the thing that was sent by Husic, this process, this authentication process, would it be the proper one or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This authentication is incorrect. The authenticity of the document cannot be certified by the person who authenticated the document and signed it. He's the assistant commander of a brigade, and the document should have been authenticated by somebody from the Corps to assure that it had arrived at the Corps Command and that it should be passed on to the units. So it's not the person that is authorised. It's strange that a document that originated in the Corps Command or the General Staff would be authenticated by a lower-ranking person, and I think that even this brigade perhaps was not even part of the 3rd Corps. I'm not sure. I didn't actually see it mentioned in the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were saying that what is authenticated is the letter by Husic and not the document signed by Delic; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, we have a misunderstanding. On condition that the authorised person that is authenticating the transcript certified this transcript, which in this case they did not, then this transcript would relate only to the information that is being passed forward with the cover letter by Husic, not the first part. That --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're asked to repeat yourself, sir, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the assumption that the person who authentified [as interpreted] the transcript, is the authorised person, this assertion that the authenticity of the transcript is certified would refer only to the document beginning from below the line on the first page and going on to the second page; so this document that is being enclosed with Husic's cover letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor or another person, could they have asked for a copy of the entire document, referring to the two acts or documents? Could it be some kind of authentication of this type, to show that it is true to the original?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand you. Really, I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is when it was authenticated. Is there any date showing when it was done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, as far as I'm concerned, it's not at all clear. I'm still in the dark as to this authentication process. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, Witness, in our language the authentication of a document is not -- is not a certification of the correction of the transcript, of the correctness of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, what I understand as an authentication of the transcript is that the person who is doing that would affirm that the contents of the transcript is authentic and true to the original document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you are saying that whether they are identical; as to whether they are authentic, that is a different question?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Bosnian language, authentication of the transcript is something that is common, and that is what is used, meaning the term signifies that the contents of the original are the same as or true to the copy or the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, in any case, the Assistant Commander for Morale of the 7th Brigade was not authorised to authenticate the transcript of a document by the General Staff or a document by the 3rd Corps; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are. Only in the event that he received a document from the 3rd Corps and was sending it to his subordinate units, to his lower unit, he could then authenticate it. If he was sending a source document to his battalions, then as somebody who received the document, he could then authenticate the transcript that was being sent to his subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, you said that you never saw this document and it never passed through the Cabinet?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It was not drafted and it did not pass through the Cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, may we put this document away now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not being tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please look at 28 -- P2809.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it P2089? I'm looking at --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 809, 2809. Your Honours, it is the document we have on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please have a look. You commented on this in paragraph 28 of your statement. This is about the dismantling of the El Mujahedin Detachment. It's an order. You've seen this document a number of times, haven't you? You looked at it several times as you were being proofed for your evidence in court. You will agree with me that the final decision on the dismantling of the El Mujahedin Detachment is a result of the Dayton Accords; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. That's what the preamble of the document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could Madam Vidovic please be asked not to overlap with the witness, because we can't hear the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I got no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I believe that the interpreters did not interpret the last answer by the witness because there was an overlap, and so you are kindly requested to consider again to be careful not to overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in this situation I really don't know how I was overlapping with the witness. I was not. I see what it says, but really the interpreters should try harder. Let me see what the last question was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I believe we discussed this. I asked you about this, that -- this order being a result of the Dayton Accords being signed, and you said that this was true; is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I said what the preamble said of the order and what whoever was drafting the order was invoking, what the basis was for this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General Delic found it very important to comply with the agreement and as far as it concerned the El Mujahid Detachment, and to comply with the terms of the Dayton Accords in general; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Command Staff found it very important to resolve, as painlessly and as simply as possible, this problem involving the El Mujahedin Detachment, and this was no simple problem, was it?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Commendations and awards were a way to make the process of dismantling the unit as simple as possible and to bring it to as speedy a conclusion as possible; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, of course, if you're dismantling the unit, they're much happier leaving with some sort of a commendation rather than without one, walking away empty-handed, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. In other words, it would be simpler for them to accept this decision; they would not stir up any trouble or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I want to ask you specifically about the Golden Lily award or decoration, which is another thing that you commented on in your statement. This award or decoration is normally awarded for important contributions to the resistance in armed -- resistance to armed aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a token of appreciation for personal courage and personal contributions made to the armed struggle against the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please put the document that we have before us away, please, and I want the witness now to look at D666.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is the third document in a row that we have been seeing -- that we have seen that has not been tendered. What is the purpose of using these documents if they are not getting into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these are documents that the witness commented on in his statement. I do not wish to find myself facing a situation where these documents are being tendered later on through a witness who will be unable to explain the importance of the document, the substance of the document, or its authenticity, and I believe I am perfectly within my rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why don't they get them tendered through this witness who is commenting on the authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I could go without, but I think this is something that the OTP showed the witness in a limited way. That's true. But this is not a document that I want to become one of the exhibits. I just want the witness to comment on the document in much the same way that the OTP had him comment on it. I don't know. If you see it fit, perhaps I could move for this to be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When we are at the judgement and a document is being spoken about and we want to check what document that was and what that document was saying, and it is not on the record, what are we going to do? We just disregard that part of the evidence because the document is not there? And it means we have been wasting time this whole afternoon taking down this evidence, because the documents that are supposed to go with this evidence are not on record.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think you should raise this with the OTP, why, because these are 92 ter statements, and then what they do is attach a large number of documents to this set. They are tendered and exhibited. Some of these are highly detrimental, at least potentially, to my client. I want this witness to shed light on this document, but it's certainly not a document that I wish to tender. And this is definitely not a waste of time. I think I know what will happen at the end. They will try to exhibit this from the Bar table or through a different witness, who will confirm a small portion of the document, and I will end up not having a comment on this document from a person who may be, in this case, in a position to significantly contribute to our understanding of the document, and I really do not believe that this is a waste of time, this entire exercise. What if tomorrow, for example, the OTP, as I'm sure they'll do, starts tendering documents through a different witness or from the Bar table?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If they do that and the witness through whom they are trying to tender the document doesn't know anything about that document, then you have the right to object, because they've left the witness who could have done so and didn't use him to tender the document. And I would imagine that you would be perfectly within your right to object. Now, if the documents were attached to his statement and they were not used by the Prosecution, and they are not also used by you, then we don't -- they're not tendered into evidence. However, if they are used and not tendered, then that creates a problem, at least for me. For me, my understanding is any document that is attached to a statement, unless specifically tendered, it's not tendered and it's not used in court. But once it is used, I expect to see it at the time of judgement writing. However, you may go ahead, Madam. I've heard your explanation. Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would move for this document to be tendered into evidence on the basis that -- on the basis of actually the explanation that Madam Vidovic provided to Your Honours, that she wanted this witness to shed light on the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But why didn't the Prosecution tender this document when it was leading this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution attempted to tender one document that was discussed by this witness in his statement, but it met with a pretty strenuous objection from the Defence. Obviously, this witness -- the nature of this witness's explanations in relation to each of the documents that are discussed in his statement would have been similar. They're not documents that he would have probably seen. They're not documents that he has acknowledged that he saw in his capacity as the Chief of Cabinet. They're documents that he can discuss on a general level in terms of how they would have arrived at General Delic's desk for his signature and whether or not those documents -- or whether or not the signature that appeared on the documents looked like General Delic's signature. That would have been the extent of his explanation. I tried to solicit that particular explanation in relation to one document, and it met with an objection, and I didn't see any point in showing him additional documents that would have similarly met with similar objections, and it would have just been a waste of the Court's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Madam Vidovic. D666.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you see that this is a monograph, it's called, "The Golden Lily." Can we please go to page 2 of this document. It shows the persons who were actually awarded the Golden Lily between 1992 and 1995. Page 2 in the English as well, in the English. Please focus on this person, Antunovic, Stipo, Nikola-Kava, first photograph and the first name also. It says -- just a minute, please. Antunovic, Stipe, Nikola, also known as "Kava," received the war decoration, the Golden Lily, in 1994 as a member of the HVO, 110th Glorious Mountain Brigade, Operations Group 7-South" and then -- just a minute. Have you seen the photograph and the caption? I'll be showing you another one and then I'll be asking you a question?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, Your Honours, a person who was awarded the Golden Lily is a member of the HVO 110th Glorious Mountain Brigade, Operations Group 7-South. Can we please turn to the next page of the document. The same page in English. It's precisely what we see over here, "Lovric, Vinko," Ronoldo -- Ronaldo. You see he was killed on the 28th of December at Mujkica Brdo, and he was a member of the Croat Armed Forces, the HOS; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what I want to ask you about these two persons is this: I'm merely singling these two out as an example. You will agree with me that the Golden Lily was a decoration that was meant to be awarded to members of the BH Army alone?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that. The Golden Lily was awarded to members of the BH Army, to certain units of the HVO, and the HOS, who fought alongside with the units of the BH Army. But in addition to this, the Golden Lily was also awarded to other people who contributed to the armed struggle, not just members of the army. There were a number of civilians, too, who won this award, certain heads of municipalities and certain individuals who were not themselves members of the Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, may we please have a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 821.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic, I wonder what the relevance of this is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a whole number of exhibits from the OTP were in reference to members of the El Mujahid Detachment who were awarded the Golden Lily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to ask one thing. Witness, the Golden Lily was given to fighters, combatants who fought against the Serb enemy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, I think a number of these awards were also awarded in early 1993 and until the Washington Agreement was signed, and that concerned battles against the HVO. So these were not awarded for personal contribution to the struggle against the Serbs alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not what I was saying. I wasn't referring only to the Army of the Republika Srpska, but I was also talking about the people or the troops from the JNA at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but not just for courage and for their contribution to fighting the Army of Republika Srpska. Some members of the BH Army got their Golden Lilies also at the time when there was fighting going on with the HVO, early 1993 and all the way up until the Washington Agreement as the fighting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, now it's all very clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... against the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, I was interrupted in seeking to lodge my dissent against the admission of this document. It is hereby done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions about the relations between General Delic and the corps commander. You talk about this in paragraph 28 of your statement. When talking about the relations between General Delic and General Mahmuljin, it would be accurate to say, in fact, wouldn't it, that these relations had nothing unusual or exceptional about them and nothing to distinguish them from the way the relations that General Delic entertained with any other high-ranking officers?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I said that the relations between General Delic and the Commander of the 3rd Corps, General Mahmuljin, was respectful and professional, in the military way. Both were military officers, and they both knew their rights and responsibilities. During my time with the Cabinet, I certainly never noticed that the relations between the two were in any way special. They were the same as relations between the general and any other corps commander or any other subordinate commander, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Can the witness now please be shown P2131.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, have a look, please. It reads: "Information by the 3rd Corps commander," dated the 2nd of June, 1995, and then it was sent to the Presidency of the Republic of B and H, to the attention of Alija Izetbegovic, the president. Can we please look at the bottom half of the document so the witness can see the signature. That's page 2 in the English. If we can please have page 2 in the English. Right. And now we can please go back to page 1 in the English and pull the document down.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Signed by 3rd Corps commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This signature looks like General Mahmuljin's signature, but I can't establish its authenticity, and the same applies to the previous one that you asked me to look at. It certainly does look like General Mahmuljin's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, fine. Let's pull the document down a little bit, please, if we can.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you look at the handwritten bit here. It says: "Urgent via the Cabinet" -- Can we pull the English up a little, please, so we can see the translation: "Urgent via the office of the commander of the Main Staff, Sarajevo. Deliver immediately." Can we please show the document in such a way that we see the main body of the document. Thank you. This document is supposed to have reached the Cabinet at a time when you were working there; right? Could we please just zoom in so the witness can read the document.

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the document yesterday -- rather, two days ago when I spoke to the gentlemen from the OTP. I'd never seen this document before -- or, rather, it had been shown to me in Sarajevo, but the first time I read it was two days ago. This document never reached the Cabinet and was not forwarded through the Cabinet. I am certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: M'mm-hmm, all right. You do agree that were this document to be forwarded to the Cabinet, were it to reach the reception centre of the General Staff, were they to see that it was addressed to General Izetbegovic, they would have to forward it to Izetbegovic; would that not be the correct procedure to follow? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the established procedure, yes. The Communications Centre of the General Staff, whenever they received documents that were meant for someone else, for example, the Presidency, the Government, or anyone else who was not a member of the Cabinet, all those who were in communication and in touch with the Cabinet, those did not go to the Cabinet directly; rather, they would be forwarded to whoever the recipient happened to be. I have no idea why this handwritten note was put there: "Urgent via the Cabinet." I know that that's now how these were sent. It was from the Communications Centre that these documents were forwarded to whoever the addressee happened to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's leave aside the handwritten note for a minute, please. You do agree that this is not normal procedure, in terms of communication within the command-and-control system, for information like this to be forwarded to the president directly; it wasn't normal, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clear who informs the president. The commander informs the president, and that is perfectly clear, if you look at the command-and-control system. However, the institution of the commander itself is being pushed aside here. So if all of this is accurate, the 3rd Corps commander bypasses the commander and speaks directly to the president of the Presidency, and this is certainly no established procedure in the -- in military practice, this is not something that is consistent with military rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, may this document be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 822.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown 2802, P2802.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, may I interrupt you. Can we just check the dates? It looks like the English and Bosnian dates are not exactly the same. The Bosnian looks like a "5" instead of a "7".

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please lower the English. There is a portion of the document that we can't see right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, I see the date says "5 December" now. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, have a look, please. You were shown this document previously by the OTP. It's another one of those. This is another document produced by the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I spoke about this document in my statement and I said it was produced in Kakanj, not in the Cabinet itself. And one thing I find illogical about this document is that the Commander of the Supreme Command Staff is hereby granting authorisation for travel. During all of my time with the Cabinet, I don't remember the commander ever personally authorising anyone's request for travel.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You agree, don't you, that this was another document that was encrypted before it was sent? We certainly wouldn't see it, we certainly wouldn't see the signature. You said it was encrypted; right?

utterances.speaker: FERID BULJUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the upper right corner we see when it was received by the corps Communications Centre. You see that it was received on the 7th of December, 1995, and you see the signature of whoever processed the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So this was not a document produced by --
